title: an interview on feminist ethics and theory with judith butler
display_name: An Interview on Feminist Ethics and Theory with Judith Butler
abstract: in 2015 i was asked to conduct an interview with judith butler by the editorial board of kharmagas: nashriyyih falsafi-ejtema i (gadfly: persian journal of philosophy) for an august 2016 issue dedicated to the theme of identity. i conducted the interview in english, and it was translated into persian (tohidi 2016). the main readers of the journal are iranian intellectuals and activists, including many feminists. butler is known and respected as a feminist philosopher among iranian intellectuals. her seminal book gender trouble was translated into persian (butler 1999, 2006).the questions i posed reflect my own intellectual and political concerns as a feminist scholar and activist of iranian background. but they also address transnational questions that remain relevant to feminist studies and middle east studies and are within the realm of butler s published works and expertise. i submitted all the interview questions by e-mail in october 2015, and butler submitted her responses in april 2016. the interview therefore lacks the natural back-and-forth flow and dynamic interaction of a more synchronic conversation. i think that such interviews are important for intensifying intellectual discussion between feminists in the global north and the global south, including regarding the continuing barriers to building alliances. such exchanges should problematize not only binary understandings of gender and sexuality but also the simplistic binary of the west against the rest by exploring the current geopolitics of scattered masculinist hegemonies at the local as well as global contexts. actively crossing these divides is more urgent with the growing global trend of right-wing ethnocentric nationalisms and populisms, and religious fundamentalisms.nayereh tohidi:thanks to our firsthand praxis and also the work of some feminists, especially feminists of color in the west or in the global south, such as sociologist patricia hill collins and critical race theorist kimberl crenshaw, many of us academics and activists have adopted an intersectional approach and try to avoid universal statements that assume woman as a unified class. furthermore, thanks to feminist philosophers like yourself, especially your groundbreaking book, gender trouble, we have moved away from binary conceptions of gender and sexuality that limited our understanding of gender on the basis of oppositional notions of masculinity and femininity. we have thereby become better aware and critical of pervasive heteronormative assumptions in feminist theory. having said that, my first question is ostensibly simple: how would you define feminism?judith butler: i am not sure that i can define feminism. in my mind, feminism is a historical movement, so we have to ask, what has it become and what is it becoming? and we have to ask about the place and time of its articulation. at a minimum, feminism opposes inequality, exploitation, and violence, and it recognizes that women suffer disproportionately from illiteracy and poverty. i try to register definitions of feminism when i come across them, but i do not understand myself in a position to define feminism. it could be that i do not want feminism to have a fixed definition, but that is because i want it to remain alive, becoming more expansive, inclusive, and powerful.nt:in the preface to the second edition of gender trouble (1999), while you emphasize the irreducible complexity of sexuality, you state, i continue to hope for a coalition of sexual minorities that will transcend the simple categories of identity, a coalition that will counter and dissipate the violence imposed by restrictive bodily norms (xxvi). do you also advocate for such coalition building among women in general? in spite of sexual, racial, class, ethnic, and national differences among women, do you agree that there are enough common issues and concerns (including violence against women and practices such as forced marriage, genital mutilation, forced veiling, and forced prostitution) that make negotiated local, national, transnational, and even global coalition building among women possible and even necessary? if yes, can this happen without some sense of solidarity and feminist identity formation?jb: here is where the intersectional approach that you mention in your first question becomes important. my sense is that when we refuse the unified category of women, and accept that other forms of power traverse the categories of gender, we stand a chance of a more complex analysis and alliance. i do not see that we need a feminist identity formation, but rather a set of feminist commitments that are revised in light of the different geopolitical demands of the feminist movement. a practice and a movement, even an alliance, do not require an identity. sometimes we have to let identities go or, at least, not let them serve as organizing principles of a movement, so that we can make alliances. and we make alliances not for the purposes of building identities, but for building movements.i do think that women have to work together, but i am not sure those alliances cannot include men. i think they can and should include trans women, who belong to the category as much as i do.nt:in a 1998 interview that included elizabeth grosz, you said the term essentialism was used quite easily in criticizing, for instance, luce irigaray (cheah et al. 1998). how has your understanding of essentialism changed and what it is today?jb: i am not sure that issue is as strongly debated as it was all those years ago. at the time, there was a fear that some feminist philosophies still believed that biology is destiny, that whatever distinct reproductive functions women have implies distinct forms of sexuality or even specific kinds of work for women. so the turn to social construction tended to underemphasize the biological. i understand now that many feminists want to be able to think carefully about biology without assuming that biology is destiny, and this has given rise to an impressive group of feminist philosophers and anthropologists of science. i worried that irigaray tended to presume a heterosexual structure for desire, and that the feminine was established by virtue of heterosexual difference. not everyone agrees with that reading.nt:in the same 1998 conversation, you and drucilla cornell argue that irigaray deploys the feminine not in an essentialist but in an unabashedly utopian manner that is beyond whatever presently intelligible category or concept we have. and it is through this beyond, this utopian and imaginary femininity, that we can get to a different kind of ethics, a feminist ethics. how have your views changed since then and what is your latest take on this imaginary femininity ? how you would explain feminist ethics to an iranian readership or characterize it more generally?jb: i have tried to become more sympathetic to this view, namely, that the feminine stands for the future or that it designates a future horizon. but still it is not my view. i am aware that for so many women who do not identify with femininity or for so many men who do identify with femininity, these matters are complex and we cannot always link the category of women with the feminine. it is not just about how women appear or what they want, but about whether the category of women operates in a way that articulates hope for the future or forecloses any such hope. in this sense, then, i am very grateful to transgender movements that have gone further in recent years than i was able to go before to elaborate conceptions of gender that make life more or less livable. i guess this last question what are the conditions of livability is most important to me at this time. i think that feminist ethics, and perhaps any ethic, should be committed to making life more livable for as many people as possible. we should embrace a principle of the equal value of life and support the equal claim on livability. this relates to women, but also to refugees, to prisoners, and to all those who are denied basic rights.nt:at times human/women s rights have been instrumentalized or co-opted by the right for hegemonic and imperial goals at the international level. at the same time, human/women s rights have been dismissed as western by local, native, and national patriarchal and despotic forces to justify gross violation of civil and human rights of women and sexual minorities. islamic fundamentalists or religious conservatives in general and also secular despotic forces usually do this by invoking the notion of cultural relativism. how can we uphold an inclusive and universal conception of human/women s rights without losing our sensibilities of cultural, historical, and contextual differences?jb: i understand that human rights, even women s human rights, have often been invoked to impose a western set of norms on non-western regions and to that extent represent a culturally imperialist force. but i have also seen forms of global solidarity on issues such as violence against women and the parenting rights of single women and lesbians that have been quite useful for many activists in their local contexts. the movement against violence against women in south america does not for the most part base their human rights claims on dominant north american paradigms. for populations that had to throw off dictators and reclaim democracy, sometimes human rights discourse was necessary.so human rights can work in the service of imperialism, but also against colonialism or authoritarian rule, and that makes it a complex instrument. we always have to ask about the politics of human rights in this or that context: how does it work? how does it fail to work? so there should be no human rights without a politics of human rights.for those oppressive regimes that conveniently make use of relativist arguments, i think they should be refused. after all, we can agree on general principles about justice, equality, and freedom. but we can then immediately ask, what do those terms mean in this or that context? in other words, those may not be the exact words to use, and other words may do that work better. principles like this have to be translated, but they also have to be elaborated culturally. that is not relativism, but neither is it the imposition of abstract norms born in the west on regions and movements that prefer a different set of vocabularies and practices. my sense is that even absolute principles have to be able to withstand the demand for translation. they appear differently in different languages, and there is, as ludwig wittgenstein says, a family resemblance among such terms.nt:in your book undoing gender (butler 2004), you considered the legalization of gay marriage to be a starting point for changes in attitudes and policies toward those who live in alternative family arrangements. but you also talked about a dilemma between achieving social recognition and legal equality for homosexual couples, on the one hand, and the possibility of rendering other sexual arrangements illegible, on the other. do you still have that concern, and if so how, politically and practically, can it be resolved, and what would be transnational and global implications of the legalization of gay marriage in america and europe?jb: in general, it is good that gay marriage is increasingly accepted, since it extends principles of equality in that domain. we know as well that there is a serious backlash against gay marriage in many parts of the world. it is a civil right, a personal right, and anyone should be able to marry if one wishes. my concern was not only that marriage becomes the singular way of thinking about legitimate sexual relations, and that is a problem, but that our intimate relations are increasingly mediated by state power that is also a problem. at that time, i asked, why do we want to have the recognition of the state? is it that the recognition of the state is more valuable than forms of recognition that take place outside the law, in communities that are formed in extralegal spheres? it may be that we think that only with state recognition will gay and lesbian people have legal protection for their relationships. but in some legal systems, one can gain protection through other means. i do believe that the aim of feminism to affirm modes of sexual freedom that do not conform to the marriage norm has been partially lost as marriage becomes a stronger norm. gay, lesbian, bisexual, and queer people also sought to expand the imaginary domain of intimate ties, ties of interdependency. those more experimental forms of kinship have become backgrounded. here again, such ties make life livable, and sometimes marriage can make a life unlivable. so it is important to keep this question open to debate.nt:some look at feminisms from a sort of developmental perspective. they say that in societies such as afghanistan, saudi arabia, and even iran, people are still struggling to come to terms with some basic human rights principles and certain emancipatory ideals of the enlightenment and modernity. for them, certain postmodern ideas can paralyze any feminist strategizing, solidarity, and political actions toward social change. for instance, in line with drucilla cornell (cheng et al. 1998, 24), they too may argue: how can we completely do away with the gender identities, especially the category of women and femininity, since we have a symbolic order that polices and reinforces gender hierarchy and identity ? and if gender hierarchy and the policing of gender continue in western contexts despite recent relative openness and tolerance toward sexual alterities, it is much more of a challenge in less advanced or transitional societies that still perceive gender and sexual identities to be based on a rigidly dichotomous or binary opposition. they not only deny equal rights for women and sexual minorities (lgbtq) but treat them as legal and moral outcasts. in other words, some may say that your ontological argument about gender trouble, gender crisis, or sexual difference in crisis, which challenges foundational assumptions of sexual difference in feminist theory, is elitist and western. it is not very useful or applicable, at least not at this historical juncture, to feminisms that are grounded in the global south. some of these feminist critics are politically and practically more engaged with daily efforts to bring about institutional, legal, and political changes in countries like egypt or iran. they may not be as concerned with the articulation of a shared or definite ontological or epistemological commitment and thus can hardly relate to your theories. how would you respond to such arguments or criticisms?jb: if we change your question a bit, we may see a different answer. for instance, if feminists seek alliance with gay, lesbian, bisexual, and trans people, then they cannot afford to embrace established and stable ideas of gender. they have to see that gender changes historically, and that to remain within a fixed definition is an effort to stop history. if we argue that the gender binary is policed, and that is why we must stay within the gender binary, are we then accepting the fact that the police are defining our terms of identity? of course, there is a different argument that i understand. if women were to accept an ontological crisis in the category of women, they may well lose a sense of belonging or may well attract violence, both legal and extralegal. if we think about it, almost all versions of feminism have had to revise the idea of what a woman is and can be. can she marry on her own, as she wishes? can she work? can she work and study? can she work and study and have a family? can she run fast? can she carry weight? all of these very basic feminist questions have demanded that gender categories change and expand under the pressure of women s own demands. how that happens in afghanistan or iran is surely different from how it happens in chile and colombia, but i think the idea that the categories of gender are, and should be, revisable is quite basic to most feminisms. that does not have to be a western idea. those changes can and do happen within very specific languages of the family, law, or religion that do not have to adopt the language of western theory. when the question is posed, should a woman be beaten?, it presupposes a prior question: is this something women should be asked to accept as part of their necessary situation? the second question highlights the problem of how a woman s necessary situation is regarded. those who say, for instance, that beating is what women endure, and that is the way of things, naturalize a link between gender and violence: to be that gender implies having to endure that violence. so when the claim arrives that violence should not be accepted as part of her situation, and that there is nothing necessary about violence against women, we revise both the category of women and the conceptualization of violence. maybe we have to be able to track linguistic and cultural change with more nuance, with more attention to local vocabularies and abiding frameworks, so we can understand why violence is accepted, and how it can be brought into question and actively opposed.nt:finally, a question of my own concern: regardless of the flaws and biases in modern and postmodern discourses, and without conceiving of them in binary opposition, i wonder if a society or a social justice movement, including a feminist movement, can abandon modernity and adopt postmodern discourse before having built modern sociopolitical and legal institutions, that is, without having gone through the experience of liberal democracy and capitalist modernity. i ask this because i see some on the left who are properly critical of the limits of liberalism or what they call western modernity and advocate for a global grand agenda against liberal democracy, including liberal feminism, and expect feminists of all nations, from afghanistan to the united states of america, to adhere to radical, antiliberal, anticapitalist, and antiglobalization politics. i see this as a kind of anglo-centric perspective, as if all justice movements should configure their agendas based on the standpoint and priorities of the left and feminists in the united states and europe. what is your take on this?jb: i am not sure that anyone can simply abandon modernity (although modernity can take credit for abandoning many populations). for the most part modernity is part of what shapes us as subjects. similarly, i am not interested in abandoning all forms of democracy there are forms of radical democracy that incorporate some classical liberal principles that i affirm. so it is not that the postmodern postdates the modern. it is rather that many of us find ourselves living in the midst of conflicting frameworks, even conflicting intellectual time zones, and have to find our way when the methods for negotiating such complexity are hardly settled. i am quite sure that radical social justice movements have to emerge from local organizing and that the terms cannot be dictated by ostensibly vanguard movements in the west. at the same time, it may be that political discourses cross one another, and that syncretistic political vocabularies have the complexity that is needed. or it may be that political discourses are sometimes incommensurable. for instance, if we are lamenting the loss of basic social services, that is, the loss of social democracy in some parts of the globe, and then calling for the end of state power in another part, we are probably working at cross-purposes. but that conflict can become the basis of a study, a reflection, a mode of political analysis. so i am for democracy, but against those forms of democracy that advertise their commitment to abstract rights while the people they represent get poorer and more precarious all the time. i do not want the state to abandon commitments to health care, but i do not want to see the massive expansion of its securitarian powers. if that is so, i cannot say i am pro-state or antistate. it would be good to see a state for the palestinian people, for instance, but much depends on what kind of state formation that might be. maybe this notion of post simply names the fact that we have to take in our complex global reality through a series of frameworks, and that we have no ready-made framework for bringing it all together. that said, fundamental commitments to equality, to nonviolence, and against exploitation, racism, and all forms of gender and sexual discrimination, take us some way toward a consensus, even if no consensus is ever achieved without a complex, sometimes painful, practice of translation.
